title: Rhetoric and clear writing
description: The classical tools of persuasion and the plain rules that make prose easy to read.

ideas.title: The three appeals
ideas.summary: Aristotle held that we persuade through character, emotion and reasoning: ethos, pathos and logos.
links: latin-and-greek-roots:Greek roots for words and knowing

items.q: In Aristotle's account of rhetoric, what is ethos?
items.a: Persuasion through the speaker's character and credibility

items.q: In Aristotle's account of rhetoric, what is pathos?
items.a: Persuasion by appeal to the audience's emotions

items.q: In Aristotle's account of rhetoric, what is logos?
items.a: Persuasion through reasoning and evidence

items.q: A speaker mentions her twenty years as a surgeon before giving medical advice. Which of Aristotle's three appeals is she using?
items.a: Ethos

items.q: In classical rhetoric, what is kairos?
items.a: The right or opportune moment to say something

ideas.title: Figures of speech
ideas.summary: Named patterns of repetition, contrast and comparison are what make a sentence stay in the mind.

items.q: Churchill's "we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds" uses which figure of repetition?
items.a: Anaphora: repeating the same words at the start of successive clauses

items.q: "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country." Which figure reverses its terms like this?
items.a: Chiasmus (strictly, antimetabole)

items.q: What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
items.a: A simile compares using "like" or "as"; a metaphor says one thing is another

items.q: What is litotes?
items.a: Understatement that affirms something by denying its opposite, as in "not bad"

items.q: In rhetoric, what is a tricolon?
items.a: A series of three parallel words, phrases or clauses, as in "veni, vidi, vici"

items.q: What is metonymy?
items.a: Naming something by a thing closely associated with it, as "the crown" for the monarchy

ideas.title: Plain style
ideas.summary: Clear prose prefers short words, active verbs and concrete nouns, and cuts whatever does no work.

items.q: Which short style guide by Strunk and White contains the rule "omit needless words"?
items.a: The Elements of Style

items.q: Which 1946 essay by George Orwell argues that stale, vague prose corrupts thought?
items.a: Politics and the English Language

items.q: In grammar, what is the difference between the active and the passive voice?
items.a: In the active the subject does the action; in the passive the subject receives it

items.q: Put this sentence into the active voice: "Mistakes were made by the committee."
items.a: The committee made mistakes.

items.q: In writing advice, what is a nominalization?
items.a: A verb or adjective turned into an abstract noun, such as "implementation" for "implement"

ideas.title: Structure and the reader
ideas.summary: Good writing is arranged for the reader: the point comes early and each paragraph does one job.

items.q: In a paragraph, what is a topic sentence?
items.a: The sentence, usually the first, that states the paragraph's main point

items.q: What does the journalists' warning "don't bury the lede" mean?
items.a: Put the most important point at the start, not deep inside the piece

items.q: What is the curse of knowledge, which Steven Pinker blames for much unclear writing?
items.a: The difficulty of imagining what it is like not to know something that you know

items.q: In writing, what is parallel structure?
items.a: Giving the items in a list or pair the same grammatical form
